[Bug]: Kimi-K3 MoE padding floor scales with TP - crashes `deep_gemm_mega_moe` at TP>=16 and pins per-GPU weight memory at ~120GB ### Your current environment ### Summary `KimiMoE.__init__` pads `moe_intermediate_size` up to `min_moe_intermediate_per_partition * tp_size`. Because the pad target scales *with* `tp_size`, `padded // tp_size` is identically `min_moe_intermediate_per_partition` — the per-partition size saturates and stops decreasing as GPUs are added. This has two consequences for `moonshotai/Kimi-K3`, both of which only appear at TP >= 16: 1. An unguarded attribute write crashes model init when `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe` is used. 2. Per-GPU MoE weight memory is pinned at ~120 GB regardless of TP, so adding nodes does not reduce it. Neither is hardware-specific. The published recipe is TP=8 on 8x GB300, which is exactly the case that skips the padding branch — which is likely why this hasn't surfaced. ### The code — `vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/model.py:493-502` ```python self.padded_moe_intermediate_size = moe_intermediate_size min_moe_intermediate_per_partition = getattr( config, "min_moe_intermediate_per_partition", 256 ) if self.tp_size > 1: moe_intermediate_per_partition = moe_intermediate_size // self.tp_size if moe_intermediate_per_partition < min_moe_intermediate_per_partition: self.padded_moe_intermediate_size = ( min_moe_intermediate_per_partition * self.tp_size ) ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug The padded value is what is actually handed to the experts (`model.py:600` for MegaMoE, `model.py:612` for `FusedMoEFactory`), so the memory is genuinely allocated; the pad region is only zeroed afterwards. ### Symptom 1 — AttributeError with `deep_gemm_mega_moe` `model.py:634-647` runs whenever padding engaged: ```python if self.padded_moe_intermediate_size != moe_intermediate_size: w13_weight = getattr(self.experts, "w13_weight", None) if w13_weight is None: w13_weight = getattr(self.experts, "w13_weight_packed", None) ... self.experts.moe_config.intermediate_size_per_partition_unpadded = ( # <-- unguarded moe_intermediate_size // self.tp_size ) ``` With `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe`, `self.experts` is a `KimiK3MegaMoEExperts`, which extends `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExperts(nn.Module)` — `moe_config` does not exist anywhere in that class. Every rank dies during `load_model`: ``` File "vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/model.py", line 593, in __init__ self.experts.moe_config.intermediate_size_per_partition_unpadded = ( File "torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 1967, in __getattr__ raise AttributeError( AttributeError: 'KimiK3MegaMoEExperts' object has no attribute 'moe_config' ``` (Line 593 is from the `vllm/vllm-openai:kimi-k3` image; the same statement is at line 645 on `main` as of d31de3c421.) Incidentally, this traceback is itself proof that the padding branch engaged: the statement only executes inside `if self.padded_moe_intermediate_size != moe_intermediate_size`. So in this run `moe_intermediate_size // self.tp_size < 256`, i.e. `self.tp_size > 12`, confirming that `tp_size` is the full 32 here and is not reduced to 1 by expert parallelism. **This reproduces with `--load-format dummy`** — the checkpoint is never read, so no 1.6 TB download is needed to verify it. On 4x8 H100 it fails in about 70 seconds, on all 32 ranks: ``` --load-format dummy --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe --enable-expert-parallel \ --tensor-parallel-size 32 --nnodes 4 --node-rank <0..3> --enforce-eager \ --max-model-len 4096 --max-num-seqs 1 ``` **This is not a Hopper-only report.** The MegaMoE *kernels* are SM100, but this crash happens in `KimiMoE.__init__` during module construction, before any kernel launches. `use_mega_moe` is set purely by `vllm_config.kernel_config.moe_backend == "deep_gemm_mega_moe"` (`model.py:765`) with no SM or platform check on that path — reaching this traceback on H100 at all demonstrates there is no such gate. The trigger is `3072 // tp_size < 256`, i.e. `tp_size >= 13`, so a 16x B200 DEP deployment at TP=16 (`3072/16 = 192`) should hit the identical crash. I don't have Blackwell hardware to confirm that, so it's worth a check. The weight lookups immediately above use `getattr` with fallbacks precisely because the two expert implementations name things differently, so the direct `moe_config` access looks like an oversight. Note that `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExperts` stores only `self.intermediate_size` and has no padded/unpadded distinction — DeepSeek-V4 always passes an unpadded size, so Kimi-K3 is the first caller to hand MegaMoE a padded one. A `getattr` guard stops the crash, but it's worth confirming whether MegaMoE needs the unpadded size for correctness or whether zeroed padding is sufficient. ### Symptom 2 — per-GPU memory does not scale with TP From `config.json`: `moe_intermediate_size=3072`, `routed_expert_hidden_size=3584`, `num_experts=896`, `num_hidden_layers=93`, `first_k_dense_replace=1` (92 MoE layers), mxfp4 4-bit + uint8 scale per group of 32 = 0.53125 bytes/param. `min_moe_intermediate_per_partition` is absent from the config, so the default 256 applies. MoE weight bytes/GPU = `3 * (padded // tp) * 3584 * 896 * 92 * 0.53125`: | TP | padded_I | per-partition I | MoE weights/GPU | |----|----------|-----------------|-----------------| | 8 | 3072 | 384 | 180.8 GB | | 16 | 4096 | 256 | **120.5 GB** | | 32 | 8192 | 256 | **120.5 GB** | | 64 | 16384 | 256 | **120.5 GB** | The identity holds under expert parallel too: each rank holds `896/ep` experts at the full padded size, and `padded/ep` is the same constant. Practical effect: 80 GB GPUs cannot run this model at any TP (TP=8 needs 180.8 GB, TP>=16 needs 120.5 GB), and there is no reachable value in between — TP must divide both `num_attention_heads=96` and `vocab_size=163840`, whose common divisors are only powers of two up to 32. The failure surfaces as a bare CUDA OOM inside `Mxfp4MoEMethod.create_weights` with nothing indicating padding as the cause. Observed with `--moe-backend marlin --load-format dummy` at TP=32, identically on 24 of 32 ranks (the other node was claimed by an unrelated job mid-run): ``` File "vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/model.py", line 550, in __init__ # experts construction (image numbering) File "vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/mxfp4.py", line 622, in create_weights torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 392.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 79.18 GiB of which 260.19 MiB is free. Of the allocated memory 77.40 GiB is allocated by PyTorch ``` Note this is a *lower* bound, not a measurement of the total: allocation was still in progress when the GPU filled, so it establishes >77.4 GB/GPU rather than confirming the predicted 120.5 GB. The prediction is falsifiable by anyone running TP=32 on >=128 GB GPUs. On Blackwell this is not a fit problem (120.5 GB fits in 180 GB), but it still means scaling past TP=16 buys no additional weight-memory headroom for KV cache or batch size. This also matches an independent report of ~130 GB/rank persisting across both TP=16 and TP=32 on 16x H200, described there as weights being "replicated rather than sharded" (https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3/discussions/136). The padding floor explains that without any replication bug. As a cross-check, SGLang serves the same checkpoint at TP=EP=32 on 32x H100-80GB with a marlin W4A16 runner and reports 59.6 GB/GPU resident weights. Unpadded, the MoE term at TP=32 would be `3 * 96 * 3584 * 896 * 92 * 0.53125 = 45.2 GB`, leaving ~14 GB for the non-MoE stack — which is the right order for it, given the replicated latent up/down projections alone are about 9 GB (`2 * 3584 * 7168 * 2 bytes * 92`) on top of the TP-sharded attention, embeddings and shared experts. So the unpadded shape appears servable on this hardware, and the floor is what makes it not fit. ### Questions 1. Is the floor a hard kernel requirement or a performance heuristic? DeepGEMM's expert path checks `intermediate_size % 128 != 0` (`deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py:318`), which suggests the real constraint is 128-alignment rather than a magnitude of 256. At TP=32 the natural per-partition size is `3072/32 = 96`, which is not 128-aligned, so *some* padding is needed — but a floor of 128 would give 60.3 GB/GPU instead of 120.5 GB. 2. Should the pad be capped at one alignment step rather than growing without bound with `tp_size`? 3. `min_moe_intermediate_per_partition` is read off the model config via `getattr` and isn't settable from the CLI. If a smaller floor is valid, exposing it would let 80 GB GPUs serve this model. 4. Independently of the above: could the padded size be logged, and a clear error raised when the padded footprint provably exceeds device memory? ### Environment - 4 nodes x 8x H100-80GB (32 GPUs), image `vllm/vllm-openai:kimi-k3`, which reports vLLM `0.1.dev19262+gb6bbf29dd.d20260727` (git sha `b6bbf29dd`, 2026-07-27). [Bug]: Packed IPC weight transfer permanently leaks the producer-side staging buffer

### Your current environment

Reproduced on torch 2.11.0+cu130 / H100 80GB; the mechanism is torch-level and not specific to a vLLM version — current `main` carries the affected code in `vllm/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py`.

### Describe the bug

`packed_ipc_producer` calls `reduce_tensor` once per staging buffer and ships the same rebuild args with every chunk; `packed_ipc_consumer` rebuilds a tensor from those args and releases it again on every chunk (it clones the unpacked tensors and drops the view). torch's cross-process IPC refcount pairs **one export with one rebuild-release cycle**: the export sets the shared counter to 1, each consumer-side release decrements it, and `torch.cuda.ipc_collect()` on the producer only reclaims a dropped buffer when the counter is exactly 0.

A multi-chunk transfer therefore drives the counter negative (1 - n_chunks), and the staging buffer becomes permanently unreclaimable once the producer drops it. Every packed weight transfer strands `packed_buffer_size_bytes` on the producer side. RL training loops that sync weights every step leak one buffer per step per producer rank until the colocated inference engine OOMs on wake.

Reading the refcount slot directly (it lives in the shared-memory file named by `ref_counter_handle` inside the rebuild args) during a two-process run shows the trajectory: export -> 1, then 0 / -1 / -2 after the first / second / third consume, and the buffer stays in `memory_allocated` through repeated `ipc_collect` calls.

The release-per-chunk consumer pattern dates back to the introduction of chunked packed transfers (), so this affects every release since.

### Minimal reproduction (single GPU, ~10s, pure torch)

```python
"""Minimal repro: sender-side CUDA IPC storage is permanently stranded when
one reduce_tensor export is consumed (rebuild + release) more than once,
which is exactly what packed weight transfer does (one export, one consume
per chunk). Run: python ipc_leak_repro.py (single GPU, ~10s)
"""
import multiprocessing as mp

import torch

BUF = 256 * 1024 * 1024


def consumer(q, done, stop):
 torch.cuda.init()
 while (item := q.get()) is not None:
 rebuild, args = item
 t = rebuild(*args) # open the IPC mapping (like packed_ipc_consumer)
 del t # release immediately (like clone-and-drop per chunk)
 torch.cuda.synchronize()
 done.put(1)
 stop.get()


def run(n_consumes):
 from torch.multiprocessing.reductions import reduce_tensor

 ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")
 q, done, stop = ctx.Queue(), ctx.Queue(), ctx.Queue()
 p = ctx.Process(target=consumer, args=(q, done, stop), daemon=True)
 p.start()
 torch.cuda.init()
 base = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()

 buf = torch.empty(BUF, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
 handle = reduce_tensor(buf) # export once: cross-process refcount = 1
 for _ in range(n_consumes): # each consume decrements once on release
 q.put(handle)
 done.get()
 del handle, buf # sender drops the buffer

 for _ in range(5): # "next rollout" = more ipc_collect calls
 torch.cuda.ipc_collect()
 torch.cuda.synchronize()
 leaked = torch.cuda.memory_allocated() - base
 print(f"export x1, consume x{n_consumes}: stranded after 5x ipc_collect = {leaked / 2**20:.0f} MB")
 q.put(None)
 stop.put(None)
 p.join(timeout=30)


if __name__ == "__main__":
 run(1) # protocol respected: reclaimed (0 MB)
 run(3) # packed-transfer pattern: 256 MB stranded forever
```

Output:

```
export x1, consume x1: stranded after 5x ipc_collect = 0 MB
export x1, consume x3: stranded after 5x ipc_collect = 256 MB
```

Driving the real `packed_ipc_producer`/`packed_ipc_consumer` across two processes (4 transfers, 3 chunks each, 64MB buffer) strands exactly one buffer per transfer: producer-side allocated grows 0 / 64 / 128 / 192 MB.

<summary>Refcount slot readout script (direct observation of the counter going negative)</summary>

```python
"""Read the cross-process IPC ref counter directly at each protocol step.

reduce_tensor's args carry (ref_counter_handle, ref_counter_offset): the
handle names a shared-memory file, the offset indexes an int64 slot. Dump
the slot value after export and after each consumer rebuild-release.
"""
import multiprocessing as mp
import os
import struct

import torch


def find_counter(args):
 flat = []

 def walk(x):
 if isinstance(x, (tuple, list)):
 for y in x:
 walk(y)
 else:
 flat.append(x)

 walk(args)
 for i, x in enumerate(flat):
 if isinstance(x, (bytes, str)) and "torch_" in str(x):
 name = x.decode() if isinstance(x, bytes) else x
 # events also live in shm files; the ref counter handle is the one
 # followed by an int offset whose file is int64-slot sized
 nxt = flat[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(flat) else None
 if isinstance(nxt, int):
 path = "/dev/shm/" + name.lstrip("/")
 if os.path.exists(path):
 yield name, nxt, path


def read_slot(path, offset):
 with open(path, "rb") as f:
 data = f.read()
 n = len(data) // 8
 vals = struct.unpack(f"<{n}q", data[: n * 8])
 window = {i: v for i, v in enumerate(vals) if v != 0 or i == offset}
 return vals[offset] if offset < n else None, len(data), window


def consumer(q, done, stop):
 torch.cuda.init()
 while True:
 item = q.get()
 if item is None:
 break
 f, a = item
 t = f(*a)
 del t
 torch.cuda.synchronize()
 done.put(1)
 stop.get()


def main():
 from torch.multiprocessing.reductions import reduce_tensor

 ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")
 q, done, stop = ctx.Queue(), ctx.Queue(), ctx.Queue()
 p = ctx.Process(target=consumer, args=(q, done, stop), daemon=True)
 p.start()

 torch.cuda.init()
 buf = torch.empty(64 * 1024 * 1024, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
 f_a = reduce_tensor(buf)
 counters = list(find_counter(f_a[1]))
 print("candidate counter slots:", [(n, off) for n, off, _ in counters])
 name, off, path = counters[0]

 def show(tag):
 val, size, window = read_slot(path, off)
 print(f"{tag:28s} slot[{off}] = {val} (file {size}B, nonzero slots {window})")

 show("after export")
 for i in range(3):
 q.put(f_a)
 done.get()
 show(f"after consume #{i + 1}")

 base = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()
 del f_a, buf
 for _ in range(5):
 torch.cuda.ipc_collect()
 torch.cuda.synchronize()
 freed = base - torch.cuda.memory_allocated()
 show("after del + ipc_collect")
 print(f"reclaimed = {freed / 2**20:.1f} MB")
 q.put(None)
 stop.put(None)
 p.join(timeout=30)


if __name__ == "__main__":
 main()
```
</details>

### Proposed fix

Import each export once on the consumer and release the mapping exactly once — PR incoming.

### 🐛 Describe the bug The [batch invariance docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/batch_invariance/) state the feature makes output "deterministic and independent of the batch size or the order of requests in a batch." With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` this holds on a **single GPU**, but **breaks under tensor parallelism**: repeating a byte-identical workload against the same unchanged engine returns non-identical logprobs (and, on near-ties, different tokens) once `tensor_parallel_size > 1`. This is *worse* than running without batch invariance, where the same workload is token-stable. I bisected it to a single compilation pass. **Disabling only `fuse_allreduce_rms` (with `torch.compile` and cudagraphs otherwise untouched) fully restores determinism.** That pass installs a **FlashInfer fused all-reduce + RMSNorm** kernel (`Enabled custom fusions: allreduce_rms`, `Auto-selected flashinfer allreduce backend: trtllm`/`mnnvl`). This is **not** the custom-all-reduce issue — the engine reports `disable_custom_all_reduce=True`, so that path is already off under batch invariance. #### Reproduction Same config run 8 times in one process (fresh engine, warm cache, nothing changes between repeats), then all-pairs compared as exact doubles. The `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard is required — TP>1 uses `spawn`, which re-imports the module. ```python import os, itertools os.environ["VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT"] = "1" from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams def main(): # tensor_parallel_size=1 is bit-stable; =4 is not. Add # compilation_config={"pass_config": {"fuse_allreduce_rms": False}} # to see determinism restored with TP=4. llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", tensor_parallel_size=4, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9, enable_prefix_caching=True) sp = SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=1, logprobs=20) prompts = [f"{'the quick brown fox ' * 50} item {i}:" for i in range(2000)] runs = [] for _ in range(8): out = llm.generate(prompts, sp, use_tqdm=False) runs.append([(o.outputs[0].token_ids[0], o.outputs[0].logprobs[0][o.outputs[0].token_ids[0]].logprob) for o in out]) groups = [] for i, r in enumerate(runs): if not any(runs[g[0]] == r and g.append(i) is None for g in groups): groups.append([i]) print(f"{len(groups)} distinct bit-exact outputs over {len(runs)} identical runs") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` Results (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, H100, vLLM 0.25.1): | config | distinct bit-exact outputs / 8 | verdict | |---|---|---| | `tensor_parallel_size=1` | 1 | deterministic | | `tensor_parallel_size=4` | 8 | **non-deterministic** | | `tensor_parallel_size=4`, `fuse_allreduce_rms=False` | 1 | deterministic (the fix) | #### Ruled out - **Not custom all-reduce ():** `disable_custom_all_reduce=True` in every TP run. - **Not concurrency ():** `--max-num-seqs 8` does not fix it under TP; TP=1 stays deterministic even at `--max-num-seqs 256`. - **Not the MoE `reduce_scatterv` path ():** this is a dense model on the all-reduce path. - **Not version-specific:** reproduces on 0.20.2 and 0.25.1. - **Not model-specific:** also reproduces on Llama-3.1-70B (dense, TP=4). - `enforce_eager=True` largely mitigates (small residual); disabling only `fuse_allreduce_rms` is the clean fix. #### Likely mechanism The fused all-reduce + RMSNorm kernel appears to reduce in an order that isn't stable run-to-run under TP. I could only narrow this from outside the engine. #### Suggested fix Disable `fuse_allreduce_rms` when `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` is set, mirroring the existing `disable_custom_all_reduce` guard in `ParallelConfig`. Happy to open a PR (I have the change and a validated repro).

Adaptive verification has a firm requirement that the attention backend must not use the CPU-side query lengths as a source-of-truth, instead using the gpu tensors (so that we can run the confidence-based assignment on the GPU without synchronizing the CPU).

Currently, it is not clear if our various Mamba decode kernels are compatible with varlen execution. We should audit the flashinfer and/or triton mamba decode kernels and check if we can run decode with a ragged batch.

If it's feasible, we should wire it up, validate correctness, evaluate performance, and merge support.

[Performance]: MM input tensors are re-broadcast to all TP workers on every request, even when the prefix cache fully covers the image tokens (~19 ms per unique image)


## Environment

- vLLM v0.25.1 (official `vllm/vllm-openai` Docker image), single API server process
- TP=4 on one node (4 GPUs), `mm_processor_cache_type: lru` (behavior identical under `shm`)
- Gemma-4-31B-IT with vision; `--mm-processor-kwargs {"max_soft_tokens": 560}` → `pixel_values` per image is `(1, 5040, 768)` fp32 ≈ **15.5 MB**
- `--limit-mm-per-prompt {"image": 32}`

## Workload

Assistant with a rolling visual-context window: each turn re-sends the same ~26 images (byte-identical, position-stable) plus one fresh frame. Prefix caching covers all history image tokens (this works great), and the mm processor cache hits 26/26 (also works great — with `lru`). Requests are therefore ~100% cached, and the encoder never runs for the history images.

## Problem

Even in that fully-cached state, TTFT grows **linearly with the number of unique images attached**: ~23 ms per unique image, of which ~19 ms is the EngineCore re-serializing each unique tensor and re-copying it into the shm broadcast ring to the TP workers — on **every request**, although the workers will never consume those tensors (their soft-token spans are entirely within the prefix-cache-covered region, so no encoder run is ever scheduled).

## Measurements (all in-pod via localhost, byte-identical resends, all shapes warm)

**1. Fully-cached TTFT floor vs unique image count** (queue = 0.0 ms, prefill ≈ 14 ms in all cases; `mm_cache_hits == queries` on every request):

| unique images | TTFT (ms) |
|---|---|
| 2 | 69 |
| 8 | 188 |
| 13 | 310 |
| 20 | 472 |
| 26 | **634** |

→ slope ≈ **23 ms per unique image**, all CPU, none of it GPU.

**2. Duplicate-image probe** — same request shape/token count, 26 image slots, but all 26 slots reference **one** image (byte-identical data URLs) vs 26 **distinct** images, everything cached in both cases:

- 26 distinct cached images: **639 ms**
- 26 copies of one cached image: **156 ms**

→ the cost is per-*unique* image, not per attached item. (Pickle's object memoization explains the collapse: the receiver cache returns the same tensor object per hash, so duplicates serialize once.)

**3. py-spy on the EngineCore during a pure cache-hit request loop** (26 distinct cached images per request): of 29.4 s sampled, **6.4 s in `shm_broadcast.enqueue`** and **4.4 s in `torch.serialization._legacy_save`** (rest is idle `sched_yield`). The API server process is nearly idle under the same load (parse layer measured separately at ~0.9 ms/image).

**4. Serializer baseline**: `MsgpackEncoder`/`MsgpackDecoder` (the path used API-server→EngineCore) round-trips the same 15.5 MB tensor in **0.01 ms** (zero-copy); `tensor.clone()` is 0.06 ms. The broadcast path's per-tensor cost is ~19 ms.

## Analysis (checked against current `main`)

- API-server→EngineCore transport is already hash-only on hits — `MultiModalFeatureSpec.data`'s docstring says it explicitly: *"Can be `None` if the item is cached, to skip IPC between API server and engine core processes"* (`vllm/multimodal/inputs.py`). This half of the design works.
- The EngineCore then re-populates the tensors from its receiver cache (`v1/engine/core.py:976`, `get_and_update_features`) and ships them to the TP workers inside `NewRequestData.mm_features` at admission (`v1/core/sched/output.py`) — per unique tensor, per request. Notably `NewRequestData` already carries `num_computed_tokens` in the same dataclass, so the information needed to skip is co-located with the thing to be skipped.
- On v0.25.1 the broadcast serializes via pickle → `torch._legacy_save` (full byte rewrite of each 15.5 MB). Current `main` routes CPU tensors through `_reduce_tensor` / out-of-band buffers (`shm_broadcast.py:823-846`), which should remove most of the serialization half — but the ring copy remains, and more fundamentally **the tensors are shipped at all** for requests whose image placeholders are fully covered by the prefix cache.

## Proposal

Attach an mm item's tensors to the **step where its encoder run is scheduled**, rather than to request admission:

- At admission the scheduler already knows `num_computed_tokens` and each mm item's placeholder span; an item whose span lies entirely within the computed prefix needs no encoder run and therefore no tensor on the workers. The scheduler already plans encoder execution explicitly (`scheduled_encoder_inputs`, `v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:679`), so tensors could travel with that instead of with `NewRequestData`.
- The receiver cache already retains tensors for the request lifetime, so preemption/recompute can still ship them lazily on demand.
- For our workload this turns ~25 shipped tensors per request into 0–1, i.e. the fully-cached floor becomes flat in image count (~4 ms/image of unavoidable parse+hash remains).

Happy to contribute a PR for this (and/or backport-friendly serializer improvements) with guidance from maintainers on the preferred shape.

## Reproduction sketch

```python
# against any TP>1 vision deployment with prefix caching + processor cache enabled:
# 1. build a chat request with N distinct images + fixed text; send twice (second send = fully cached)
# 2. build the same request but with all N image slots referencing ONE image; send twice
# 3. compare second-send TTFTs and watch vllm:mm_cache_* and queue/prefill counters:
# distinct-N grows ~linearly in N; dup-N stays near the 1-image floor; queue/prefill flat in both.
```

## 🐛 Describe the bug ### What happens On a preempted request, `MooncakeStoreConnector` stores **KV that does not belong to the key**. Those bytes are later read back by another request as a prefix-cache hit, loaded into the KV cache and attended over, which silently corrupts that request's output. ### Why The store is asynchronous. During a step the worker only pushes the store request onto `KVCacheStoreSendingThread`'s queue and returns; reading the blocks off the GPU and issuing the PUT happens later, on the background thread. Freeing the blocks takes an entirely separate path: in a following step the scheduler preempts the request, and core returns its blocks to the free pool within that same step, after which another request overwrites them. There is no synchronization between the two — nothing constrains when a queued job reads device memory relative to when its blocks are handed to someone else. The preemption notice does not help either. The earliest it can reach the worker is on the next step's connector metadata (`MooncakeStoreConnectorMetadata.preempted_req_ids`), and core has already freed the blocks in the very step that builds that metadata. In other words the blocks can be fully overwritten before the notice arrives, and with async scheduling the scheduler runs further ahead still. The only protection today is `request_finished()` returning `delay_free_blocks=True`, which covers the **normal completion** path only. Preemption goes the other way: `build_connector_meta()` calls `reset()` on the tracker, the blocks are freed immediately, and nothing knows that queued jobs still have to read them. ### Consequences 1. **Silent wrong results.** The poisoned key holds another request's KV, so a request that hits it attends over KV that is not its own and its output drifts unpredictably, with no error anywhere. 2. **It does not heal.** A key names a fixed token range, so once wrong bytes land under a key, every later request that hits the same prefix keeps being fed them. Contamination grows with uptime rather than decaying. 3. The more memory-constrained the deployment and the more it preempts, the more often this fires — which is exactly the deployment that wants an external KV store. ### How to reproduce Preemption has to actually happen. Configuration: - 2x H20, TP2, Qwen3-32B-FP8 - `--num-gpu-blocks-override 1024` (shrink the GPU cache to force preemption) - mooncake store backend, started cold - load: 96 requests / 48 concurrent / ~400-word prompts / `max_tokens=192` This configuration produces 162 preemptions in a single run. Nothing is visible from the outputs alone (wrong KV makes the text drift, it does not raise), so the determination is made by instrumentation. Two independent signals: **(1) Content fingerprints.** A store key names a fixed token range, so the KV under it is uniquely determined. The patch takes an 8-byte `D_pre` on the GPU **before** `batch_put` (the blocks still hold that key's own KV at that moment) and `D_post` on the destination blocks **after** `batch_get`. A disagreement means the bytes in the store are not the KV that key names, and they are already in a real request's KV blocks, about to be attended over. **(2) A scheduler-side block reallocation detector.** Recorded independently on the scheduler side: whether the blocks a store job references were reallocated to another request while that job was reading them. This signal never looks at the store's contents. The instrumentation, the load and the analysis scripts are at (instrumentation only, no behaviour changes): the fingerprint patch (`probes/fingerprint_on_main.patch`, applies on `643c125fa`), the preemption-forcing server config (`load/ab_serve.sh`), the synthetic load (`load/synth_load.py`, random-gibberish prompts so nothing dedups in the store and every save is a real `batch_put`), the orchestration for one run (`load/ab_run.sh`: cold master, server, poll `/health`, send the load) and the two analysers (`analysis/analyze_evi.py` for totals, `analysis/bad_dist.py` to split poisoned keys by `save_seq`). ### Measured `643c125fa` plus the instrumentation above, one run against a cold store, all 96 requests returned, 162 preemptions: | | | |---|---| | keys written with a fingerprint | 16,770 | | of those, written twice with differing content (excluded as ambiguous) | 0 | | read-backs checked | 16,788 | | **fingerprint mismatches** | **155** | | poisoned keys | 155 | | **requests that read wrong KV** | **1 / 96** | | jobs the scheduler-side detector flagged as "blocks reallocated while being read" | 25 | | preemptions | 162 | All 155 poisoned keys come from a single store job (`save_seq=125`), and that job is one of the 25 the scheduler-side detector flagged independently — two unrelated signals point at the same job. ### Relation to / describes a **secondary** problem derived from the same preemption scenario: a request that is rescheduled after preemption keeps its original req_id, and the store thread's bookkeeping only checks whether the req_id matches, so a leftover job from the retired generation spends the new generation's credit. The live save is silently dropped, the counter goes negative, the entry can never retire, `finished_sending` is never emitted and the blocks are held until KV starvation. fixes that. This issue is about the block lifetime itself: it never covered the preemption path to begin with. ## Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

[Rust frontend] /inference/v1/generate silently ignores n > 1; should reject it

With `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1`, a non-streaming request to `/inference/v1/generate` with `"sampling_params": {"n": 4, ...}` returns HTTP 200 with a **single** choice (`index: 0`). No error/warning but the other completions are silently missing.

The Rust frontend doesn't implement parallel sampling (in v1 it lives in the Python frontend, `ParentRequest` fan-out). Its OpenAI routes already reject it explicitly:

- `rust/src/server/src/routes/openai/completions/validate.rs`: `bail_invalid_request!(param = "n", "Only n=1 is supported.")` (same in `chat_completions/validate.rs`)

But the raw generate route can't: `vllm_text::SamplingParams` has no `n` field, so the key is dropped at deserialization, and `collect_generate` hardcodes one choice (`rust/src/server/src/routes/inference/generate.rs`).

## Expected behavior

`/inference/v1/generate` with `n > 1` returns a 400 `"Only n=1 is supported."`, matching the Rust OpenAI routes.

## Repro

```bash
VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B
curl -s localhost:8000/inference/v1/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
 -d '{"token_ids": [1, 2, 3], "sampling_params": {"max_tokens": 5, "n": 4}, "stream": false}' \
 | jq '.choices | length' # 1, expected: 4 choices or a 400
```

## Context

Found in , which fixes the Python-frontend counterpart of this bug (dropped choices under `CUMULATIVE` output kind) and skips its regression test under the Rust frontend. Suggested fix: capture `n` at the route level (e.g. a `#[serde(flatten)]` wrapper around `SamplingParams` in `generate/types.rs`) and reject in `generate/validate.rs`.

[Bug]: DSpark scheduling using an overly conservative input budget ### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug The scheduler charges each DSpark request `num_new_tokens + K - 1`, where `K` is `num_speculative_tokens`. However, the target/context tokens and the fixed-size draft query block are processed in separate stages. Combining them into one budget can unnecessarily restrict scheduling. For example, assume: ```text max_num_batched_tokens = 16 num_speculative_tokens = 4 2 requests, each scheduling 8 prefill tokens ``` Both requests fit the two stages: ```text target/context stage: 8 + 8 = 16 tokens DSpark query stage: 4 + 4 = 8 tokens ``` Current accounting charges `8 + (4 - 1) = 11` for the first request, so the two requests cannot be admitted in full despite fitting both stages. This may also affect other speculative methods. A possible fix is to keep target and draft-input budgets separate, with each method defining its draft-stage input cost. We may be missing some intended scheduling semantics; we are validating this experimentally and exploring a fix. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

[Bug]: --headless does not load custom reasoning parser plugins

### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Relevant environment details</summary>

```text
OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (aarch64)
Python: 3.12.13
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cpu
vLLM: 0.25.1
```

The failure occurs while constructing `VllmConfig`, before workers or accelerator resources are initialized. I reproduced it dynamically with vLLM 0.25.1 and confirmed that vLLM main at commit `16cfe728d8d0bc3cd4a8397db0f392dd52a2c109` still has the same `run_headless()` ordering.

</details>

### Describe the bug

`vllm serve --headless` does not import the file passed through `--reasoning-parser-plugin` before creating the engine config. If `--reasoning-parser` names a parser registered by that plugin, headless startup fails with `KeyError`.

This affects remote/headless ranks used by multi-node data-parallel deployments. It was originally observed in vLLM Ascend issue , but the failing path is in vLLM core and does not depend on the accelerator backend.

Create a minimal parser:

```python
# /tmp/custom_reasoning_parser.py
from vllm.reasoning import ReasoningParser, ReasoningParserManager


@ReasoningParserManager.register_module("custom_headless")
class CustomHeadlessReasoningParser(ReasoningParser):
 reasoning_start_str = "<think>"
 reasoning_end_str = "</think>"

 def extract_reasoning_streaming(self, *args, **kwargs):
 return None

 def extract_reasoning(self, model_output, request):
 return None, model_output
```

Then start a headless rank. The command does not require the DP head rank to reproduce the early failure:

```bash
timeout 60s vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \
 --headless \
 --data-parallel-size 2 \
 --data-parallel-size-local 1 \
 --data-parallel-start-rank 1 \
 --data-parallel-address 127.0.0.1 \
 --data-parallel-rpc-port 29550 \
 --reasoning-parser custom_headless \
 --reasoning-parser-plugin /tmp/custom_reasoning_parser.py
```

Observed result:

```text
 File "vllm/entrypoints/cli/serve.py", line 180, in run_headless
 vllm_config = engine_args.create_engine_config(
 File "vllm/config/vllm.py", line 1484, in __post_init__
 self.reasoning_config.initialize_token_ids(self.model_config)
 File "vllm/config/reasoning.py", line 77, in initialize_token_ids
 parser_cls = ReasoningParserManager.get_reasoning_parser(
 File "vllm/reasoning/abs_reasoning_parsers.py", line 245, in get_reasoning_parser
 raise KeyError(
KeyError: "Reasoning parser 'custom_headless' not found. Available parsers: ..."
```

Expected result: the plugin is imported before engine config construction, so the headless rank proceeds to worker launch/DP handshake instead of raising `KeyError`.

The regular API server path already has the required ordering:

```python
# vllm/entrypoints/openai/api_server.py
if args.reasoning_parser_plugin and len(args.reasoning_parser_plugin) > 3:
 ReasoningParserManager.import_reasoning_parser(args.reasoning_parser_plugin)
```

`run_headless()` instead calls `AsyncEngineArgs.create_engine_config()` directly. During `VllmConfig.__post_init__`, `ReasoningConfig.initialize_token_ids()` resolves the configured parser before the plugin is imported anywhere else.

As a control, explicitly calling `ReasoningParserManager.import_reasoning_parser(plugin_path)` before `create_engine_config(headless=True)` succeeds and produces an enabled reasoning config.

A narrow fix would import `args.reasoning_parser_plugin` in `run_headless()` before `AsyncEngineArgs.create_engine_config()`. Importing it from the `StructuredOutputsConfig` validator would be broader and would reintroduce the duplicate-registration/programmatic-registration problem removed by .

[Bug]: GLM-5.2 FP8 on 8×H200 dies with runtime CUDA OOM in sparse_decode_fwd

### 🐛 Describe the bug

 ## Summary

 On the FlashMLA sparse **fp8 mixed-batch** path, the sparse decode kernel allocates a workspace that
 scales linearly with `--max-num-batched-tokens` and is **not bounded by any workspace limit and not
 accounted for during startup memory profiling**. The server starts fine, serves for days, then dies
 with a runtime `torch.OutOfMemoryError` inside `flash_mla_cuda.sparse_decode_fwd` the first time a
 batch gets large enough. The OOM kills EngineCore, so every in-flight request fails with
 `EngineDeadError` and the process exits.

 This is not KV-cache pressure: **GPU KV cache usage was 2.0–5.4%** in the minute before the crash,
 with at most 8 concurrent requests.

 The mixed-batch path is selected automatically whenever per-rank head count < 32, i.e. exactly the
 common high-TP configurations. 

 ## Repro

 ```bash
 vllm serve /models/GLM-5.2-FP8 \
 --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
 --enable-expert-parallel \
 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
 --max-model-len 262144 \
 --max-num-seqs 32 \
 --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 \
 --speculative-config.method mtp \
 --speculative-config.num_speculative_tokens 5
 # NOTE: --gpu-memory-utilization left at its 0.90 default
 ```

 Then drive mixed prefill+decode traffic until a step fills the token budget. In our case it ran
 ~61 hours before dying during a burst (prompt throughput ~3.6k tok/s, 8 running requests).

 ## Error

 All 8 workers hit it in the same step:

 ```text
 (Worker_TP0_EP0 pid=751) ERROR [multiproc_executor.py:1000] Traceback (most recent call last):
 ...
 File "vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py", line 812, in forward_impl
 attn_out, lse = self.impl.forward_mqa(mqa_q, kv_cache, attn_metadata, self)
 File "vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashmla_sparse.py", line 886, in forward_mqa
 attn_out = self._forward_fp8_kv_mixed_batch(
 File "vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashmla_sparse.py", line 772, in _forward_fp8_kv_mixed_batch
 _attn_out, _ = self._fp8_flash_mla_kernel(
 File "vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashmla_sparse.py", line 803, in _fp8_flash_mla_kernel
 out, lse = flash_mla_with_kvcache(
 File "vllm/third_party/flashmla/flash_mla_interface.py", line 158, in flash_mla_with_kvcache
 out, lse, new_tile_scheduler_metadata, new_num_splits = flash_mla_cuda.sparse_decode_fwd(
 torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 8.00 GiB.
 GPU 0 has a total capacity of 139.80 GiB of which 6.40 GiB is free.
 Including non-PyTorch memory, this process has 133.39 GiB memory in use.
 Of the allocated memory 124.39 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, with 3.23 GiB allocated in
 private pools (e.g., CUDA Graphs), and 5.01 GiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.

 (EngineCore pid=614) ERROR [core.py:1233] EngineCore encountered a fatal error.
 (APIServer pid=1) ERROR [serving.py:812] vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError:
 EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace (above) for the root cause.
 ```

 The 8.00 GiB is exactly `max_num_batched_tokens x index_topk x index_head_dim`

 ```
 32768 x 2048 x 128 x 1 byte = 8,589,934,592 B = 8.00 GiB
 ```

 
 ### Root cause: the mixed-batch path bypasses the workspace bound that the separate path uses

 `vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashmla_sparse.py` (line numbers from `main` @ `a014e35f38`):

 ```python
 MIN_HEADS_FOR_BF16_PREFILL = 32 # L63
 self.fp8_use_mixed_batch = self.num_heads < MIN_HEADS_FOR_BF16_PREFILL # L307

 def get_prefill_workspace_size(max_model_len: int): # L221
 # Memory usage: 5 * max_model_len * 576 * 2 bytes
 # This fits nicely below the typical MoE workspace size of >2GB so this is "free"
 return max_model_len * 5
 ```

 * The **separate prefill/decode** path is bounded — it computes `max_prefill_buffer_size` from
 `get_prefill_workspace_size(...)` and *"Chunk[s] prefill requests to fit within workspace size"* (L451-456).
 * The **mixed-batch** path is not. Its own docstring says it *"treats all tokens as one batch"*, and
 `_forward_fp8_kv_mixed_batch` does `q.unsqueeze(0)` / `topk_indices.unsqueeze(0)` over the full
 flattened token count with no chunking and no reference to the workspace manager.

 So the one path that has no memory bound is the one selected for every config with < 32 heads/rank.

 Additionally, this allocation appears not to be captured by startup memory profiling: `profile_run`
 executes a dummy prefill before the KV cache exists, so the fp8 sparse **decode** kernel never runs
 and its workspace is never reflected in the `gpu_memory_utilization` budget. (Inferred from the
 failure timing — I have not traced `profile_run` directly.) The practical effect is that
 `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90` is unsafe here even though vLLM's own accounting says it fits:
 PyTorch took 124.39 GiB of its 125.82 GiB budget, leaving 6.40 GiB against an 8.00 GiB request.

 MTP compounds it: `num_speculative_tokens 5` puts 6 query tokens per sequence into each decode step,
 so mixed batches reach the token cap much sooner than `max_num_seqs` alone suggests.

That seems more valuable than any single grammar fix, and I'd be glad to help with it if there's interest. ## Possibly related - **** — I believe this bug is a sufficient cause of that one, **conditional on those requests having used `tool_choice="required"`** (the question @jimmywuwu asked there and which is still unanswered). The chain, verified on 0.26.0 and 0.27.1: 1. `Gemma4EngineToolParser.adjust_request` skips the structured-output constraint for required/named choice (), so the model emits its **native** scaffold — checked directly: `structured_outputs` is `None` after `adjust_request`. 2. If that scaffold uses the bare opener, the parser extracts nothing → `tool_calls == []`. 3. `serving.py` (~L1008) takes the `is_required_tool_choice` branch → `content or ""`, `tool_calls=[]`. 4. `serving.py` (~L1073): `is_finish_reason_tool_calls = auto_tools_called or (tool_choice == "required" and output.finish_reason == "stop")` → `False or True` → **`finish_reason = "tool_calls"`**. Result: `finish_reason="tool_calls"`, `tool_calls=[]`, `content=""` — 's exact reported signature. Note steps 3–4 are read from `serving.py` rather than observed on a live server; steps 1–2 are executed. This also offers a simpler explanation for two things noted there. **"Retrying usually succeeds"** follows directly: the opener is a per-sample choice, so a retry re-rolls it and usually lands on `call:`. And the **apparent concurrency correlation** is what a low-rate per-request event looks like when traffic increases — more requests, more chances to hit it — rather than a race. Two checks would settle it: (a) confirm whether those requests used `tool_choice="required"`, and (b) log raw `output.text` on failure and grep for `<|tool_call>:` versus `<|tool_call>call:`. Under `tool_choice="auto"` a bare opener yields `finish_reason="stop"`, which would *not* match that report — so if the traffic was `"auto"`, these are different bugs. - (closed) — earlier gemma4 opener/token-leak issue, but its repros show the `call:`-bearing form only, so the bare opener was never in scope. - — same parser, also concurrency-correlated, different visible symptom. - — a *different* silent-failure path in the same parser (`enable_thinking` default mismatch leaves the stream in the reasoning phase, so the tool parser is never dispatched). Fixed on `main` by , unreleased as of v0.27.1. Different cause, same shape: the model's output is lost with no signal. ## Willing to contribute We are running a local fix in production (a `--tool-parser-plugin` that adds a second opener terminal). Nine days and tens of thousands of requests since deploying it, with zero occurrences of this signature against a baseline that predicted a steady trickle. Happy to open a PR with tests. One design question I would rather have settled by a maintainer before submitting: because `TOOL_PREAMBLE` silently consumes text, a plain `":"` terminal fires on the **first colon anywhere in the preamble**, so `<|tool_call>junk:get_weather{...}` would become an executable call where today it is a silent no-op. A data-only grammar change cannot express "a colon adjacent to `<|tool_call>`"; that needs a stateful normalizer in `_preprocess_feed` (which has its own hazard — the token and the colon can arrive in separate deltas). Happy to implement either; I did not want to pick that trade-off on your behalf.

[Bug]: MiMo-V2.5 chat template is auto-detected as string, reordering multimodal content

## Bug

The official `XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.5` chat template expects structured OpenAI content, but vLLM auto-detects it as `string`.

The template passes `message.content` into a macro:

```jinja
{% macro render_content(message_content) %}
 {% for content in message_content %}
 ...
 {% endfor %}
{% endmacro %}

{{ render_content(message.content) }}
```

vLLM currently detects only loops directly over `message.content`, or loops over a variable literally named `content`. It therefore misses the macro parameter `message_content`:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4af586e185b028acf08312a4dee381b5998a137e/vllm/renderers/hf.py#L398-L449

## Impact

For OpenAI content ordered as:

```text
text "A" -> image -> text "B"
```

vLLM's default `string` path (`interleave_mm_strings=False`) moves the image placeholder to the front:

```text
<image-placeholder>\nA\nB
```

The official template should render:

```text
A<image-placeholder>B
```

Using the following option works around the issue:

```text
--chat-template-content-format openai
```

## Expected fix

Auto detection should follow `message.content` through macro arguments instead of depending on the macro parameter name. Please also add a MiMo-V2.5 regression test using `text -> image -> text`, verifying that `auto` matches explicit `openai`.

Related: fixed a similar case for the Rust frontend when the macro parameter is literally named `content`; MiMo uses `message_content`.

Tested against vLLM `main` at `4af586e185b028acf08312a4dee381b5998a137e` and MiMo-V2.5 revision `63651580ca774f8504f676040460aed3e1244ac1`.

### Name of failing test

tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs_e2e.py::test_prompt_logprobs_e2e_server

### Basic information

- [ ] Flaky test
- [x] Can reproduce locally
- [ ] Caused by external libraries (e.g. bug in `transformers`)

### 🧪 Describe the failing test

```text
FAILED v1/sample/test_logprobs_e2e.py::test_prompt_logprobs_e2e_server - aiohttp.client_exceptions.ClientResponseError: 500, message='Internal Server Error', url='http://127.0.0.1:45199/v1/completions'
```

Build: https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/85619 — the job failed on all 4 attempts.

In this run, lm-eval remained at 0/9501 while the observed `/v1/completions` requests returned HTTP 500; the six preceding pytest commands in the same job passed.

**Root cause:** grew Python's `LogprobsTensors` from 4 to 5 positional fields by adding `cu_num_generated_tokens_tensor`, but the Rust mirror `WireLogprobs` still has 4 fields under `Deserialize_tuple`. Every `LogprobsTensors` payload decoded by `WireLogprobs` therefore fails with:

```text
messagepack decode failed for ...EngineCoreOutputs:
array had incorrect length, expected 4
```

I reproduced the same decode failure locally in the Rust protocol layer without a GPU. A fix with regression coverage is ready.

<details>
<summary>Details: schema mismatch, failure path, and CI gap</summary>

**Schema mismatch.** Python (`vllm/v1/outputs.py`, after ):

```python
class LogprobsTensors(NamedTuple):
 logprob_token_ids: torch.Tensor
 logprobs: torch.Tensor
 selected_token_ranks: torch.Tensor
 cu_num_generated_tokens: list[int] | None = None
 cu_num_generated_tokens_tensor: torch.Tensor | None = None
```

Rust (`rust/src/engine-core-client/src/protocol/logprobs/wire.rs`):

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize_tuple, Deserialize_tuple)]
pub struct WireLogprobs {
 pub logprob_token_ids: WireNdArray,
 pub logprobs: WireNdArray,
 pub token_ranks: WireNdArray,
 #[serde(default)]
 pub cu_num_generated_tokens: Option<Vec<usize>>,
}
```

Because `LogprobsTensors` is serialized positionally, the added field is emitted even when `None`, producing a 5-element payload while Rust expects 4.

The failing job log contains the corresponding 5-element inner tuple:

```text
(RustFrontend) WARNING [transport.rs] failed to decode output message
 error=messagepack decode failed for ...::EngineCoreOutputs:
 array had incorrect length, expected 4; value fallback:
 [... ["int64",[2,3],...], ["float32",[2,3],...],
 ["int64",[2],...], nil, nil ...]
```

's diff touches 10 files, none under `rust/`. `LogprobsLists` remains 4 fields and is unaffected.

**Failure path.** The transport loop forwards decode errors downstream, but `run_output_dispatcher_loop` propagates the error with `?`, terminating the dispatcher. Subsequent completion requests then fail with HTTP 500.

**Scope.** I also checked the other Rust tuple types that decode Python output; `WireLogprobs` was the only field-count mismatch.

**Why no test caught it.** The wire shape is duplicated across the Python definition, Rust `WireLogprobs`, and `rust/src/engine-core-client/src/tests/python_compat.py`. updated only the Python definition; the fixture still encodes a 4-element tuple.

The Rust cargo test area only lists Rust paths in `source_file_dependencies`, so the Python-only change did not trigger that suite.

</details>

**Potential follow-ups:**

1. Add a Python/Rust wire-schema guard or generate `python_compat.py` fixtures from the real vLLM classes.
2. Add the relevant Python wire-definition paths to the Rust cargo job's `source_file_dependencies`.

[Bug]: M_LOG2E availability depends on build configuration in the FlashMLA extension

### Your current environment

### Environment

- Windows Server 2025
- Visual Studio Build Tools with MSVC
- CUDA/NVCC 13.2
- Python 3.12
- PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130
- SystemPanic/vllm-windows 0.25-based deployment
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
- 4 x H200 NVL GPUs

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Background

I encountered this issue while building the vllm-project/FlashMLA fork through SystemPanic/vllm-windows for a deployment on H200 NVL GPUs.

### Problem

The vLLM-specific FlashMLA extension uses `M_LOG2E` in:

 csrc/extension/sm90/dense_fp8/softmax.h
 csrc/extension/sm90/dense_fp8/pybind.cpp

For example:

 const float max_scaled = max(mi) == -INFINITY ? 0.f
 : max(mi) * (
 Scale_max ? scale : float(M_LOG2E));

`M_LOG2E` represents `log2(e)` and is commonly available in GNU/Linux build environments. Its availability is nevertheless implementation-specific.

With MSVC, the `M_*` constants are normally exposed only when `_USE_MATH_DEFINES` is defined before the relevant math header is included. The current source can therefore depend on build flags and translation-unit include order when compiled with NVCC and MSVC.

I understand that native Windows with NVCC and MSVC may not be part of the supported FlashMLA build matrix. However, removing this dependency would be a small cross-platform portability improvement and would not change the existing Linux result.

### Tested source-level fix

The FlashMLA extension built successfully after replacing `float(M_LOG2E)` with the equivalent float literal:

 - float(M_LOG2E)
 + 1.4426950408889634f

For the primary file, the tested change was:

 diff --git a/csrc/extension/sm90/dense_fp8/softmax.h b/csrc/extension/sm90/dense_fp8/softmax.h
 --- a/csrc/extension/sm90/dense_fp8/softmax.h
 +++ b/csrc/extension/sm90/dense_fp8/softmax.h
 @@
 -const float max_scaled = max(mi) == -INFINITY ? 0.f : max(mi) * (Scale_max ? scale : float(M_LOG2E));
 +const float max_scaled = max(mi) == -INFINITY ? 0.f : max(mi) * (Scale_max ? scale : 1.4426950408889634f);

The original expression explicitly converts `M_LOG2E` to a 32-bit `float`. The replacement literal is also a `float` because of the `f` suffix.

Both expressions round to the same IEEE-754 float32 value, so the tested change preserves the numerical result and does not alter the algorithm.

A project-owned named constant could avoid repeating the literal, for example:

 inline constexpr float kLog2E = 1.4426950408889634f;

### Alternative build-level workaround

The issue can also be avoided in the vLLM CMake integration by defining `_USE_MATH_DEFINES` for both FlashMLA extension targets:

 target_compile_definitions(
 _flashmla_C PRIVATE _USE_MATH_DEFINES=1
 )

 target_compile_definitions(
 _flashmla_extension_C PRIVATE _USE_MATH_DEFINES=1
 )

This is a smaller integration-specific workaround and keeps the existing source unchanged.

### Related shared-source occurrences

The same dependency on `M_LOG2E` also appears in source inherited from `deepseek-ai/FlashMLA`, including:

 csrc/api/dense_decode.h
 csrc/sm90/decode/dense/splitkv_mla.cuh
 csrc/sm90/decode/sparse_fp8/splitkv_mla.cuh
 csrc/smxx/decode/combine/combine.cu
 csrc/sm100/prefill/dense/kernel/sm100_fmha_bwd_kernel_tma_warpspecialized.hpp
 csrc/sm100/prefill/dense/kernel/sm100_fmha_bwd_mla_kernel_tma_warpspecialized.hpp

Confirmed still present on current main (`79651d6085`). ### 🐛 Describe the bug The `*_once` logging helpers (`debug_once` / `info_once` / `warning_once`) are backed by `functools.lru_cache`: ```python @lru_cache def _print_warning_once(logger: Logger, msg: str, *args: Hashable) -> None: logger.warning(msg, *args, stacklevel=3) ``` Several call sites pass a **live exception object** as a lazy format argument, e.g. `Platform.import_kernels`: ```python except ImportError as e: logger.warning_once("Failed to import from vllm._C: %r", e) ``` This has two consequences: 1. **Memory leak**: the lru_cache key retains the exception forever, and through `exc.__traceback__` every frame — and every local variable — on the path that raised it. `import_kernels` runs inside `LLM.__init__` (ModelConfig → model registry inspection → model_loader import chain), so on any platform where `import vllm._C` fails, the pinned locals include the `LLM` instance under construction. The first offline `LLM` of every process becomes permanently uncollectable: `del llm` no longer shuts the engine down, and the EngineCore subprocess survives until interpreter exit. On accelerator plugins the leaked engine keeps holding the device, so creating engines back-to-back in one process (common in test suites and notebooks) fails device initialization. 2. **Broken dedup**: each exception instance is a distinct cache key, so "once" actually logs on every occurrence. At least 9 call sites pass exceptions into `*_once` today (`vllm/platforms/interface.py`, `vllm/platforms/cpu.py` ×3, `vllm/platforms/cuda.py`, `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py` ×2, `vllm/utils/flashinfer.py`, `vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/allreduce_rms_fusion.py`). Minimal repro (no accelerator needed): ```python import gc, weakref from vllm.logger import init_logger logger = init_logger("leak_demo") class Payload: # stands in for the LLM instance under construction pass def raise_and_log(): payload = Payload() try: raise ValueError("boom") except ValueError as e: logger.warning_once("caught: %r", e) return weakref.ref(payload) ref = raise_and_log() gc.collect() print("payload alive:", ref() is not None) ``` Observed output: ```text payload alive: True ``` Expected: `payload alive: False` — the payload's only reference is a local of the returned frame, which should be collectable; instead it is pinned by the traceback of the cached exception. Regression window: v0.24 used plain `logger.warning(...)` in `import_kernels` (no cache, no leak); the switch to `warning_once` introduced the leak. How we found it: after upgrading a Neuron CI stack from vLLM 0.24 to 0.27, every test that creates two engines sequentially in one process began failing device initialization. A gc referrer walk from the undead `LLM` ended at the cached `ModuleNotFoundError("No module named 'vllm._C'")` held by an lru_cache key tuple. Suggested fix: sanitize `*_once` arguments in `_VllmLogger` — replace any `BaseException` with a hashable, traceback-free stand-in that preserves the `%s` / `%r` formatting of the original exception and compares by formatted text (fixing dedup at the same time). PR to follow. [Bug]: Out-of-vocab stop_token_ids crashes the whole engine on backends with bounds-checked index kernels (single-request DoS)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`stop_token_ids` is not validated against the vocabulary size. An out-of-vocab token id in a request is accepted unchecked and is later used as a **logits index on the device** (e.g. min_tokens / EOS masking does `logits.index_put_((rows, all_stop_token_ids), -inf)` in `vllm/v1/sample/logits_processor/builtin.py`). On backends whose index kernels perform device-side bounds checking, a single such request crashes the entire engine with an unrecoverable device exception.

Reproduced end-to-end on vLLM 0.23.0 + vllm-ascend 0.23.0rc1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (vocab 129280), PD-disaggregated deployment (MooncakeHybridConnector + MTP), CANN 9.1.0:

```
# request
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}], "stop_token_ids": [151645], "max_tokens": 300}

# device error (all 8 TP ranks die simultaneously)
Index out of range in dimension 1: index value 151645 exceeds bounds 129280!
[ASSERT] .../ascendc/index_check/index_check.h:130: Assertion `(idx < bound)' failed.
fault kernel_name=IndexCheck_int32_high_performance_1
RuntimeError: vector core exception, retCode=0x31
```

The prefill instance dies completely (HTTP 500 for all subsequent requests). 151645 is `<|im_end|>` of the older DeepSeek V3 tokenizer; DeepSeek-V4-Flash's vocab is 129280, so clients reusing stale token ids hit this trivially.

Trigger conditions (all verified experimentally):
1. `stop_token_ids` contains an id `>= vocab_size` — passes `_verify_common` which only checks the type (`vllm/sampling_params.py`)
2. The id reaches a device-side indexing path. This happens whenever `min_tokens > 0` (`MinTokensLogitsProcessor.apply` / `apply_with_spec_decode` register `params.all_stop_token_ids` and index logits with them). Note the PD proxy example scripts rewrite prefill requests to `max_tokens=1, min_tokens=1` (`load_balance_proxy_server_example.py`), which activates this path for **every** request going through the proxy
3. Backend performs bounds checking on index ops (Ascend CANN 9.1.x inserts IndexCheck kernels; older CANN 9.0.1 silently corrupts neighboring logits instead — arguably worse)

On CUDA the same request "works" only because out-of-bounds `index_put_` semantics are luck-dependent; on NPU with CANN 9.1 it is a guaranteed device-level crash. Either way the id can never match a sampled token, so rejecting it upfront loses nothing.

`logit_bias` and `allowed_token_ids` are already validated against the vocabulary in `SamplingParams.verify()`; `stop_token_ids` is the one unchecked entry point into `all_stop_token_ids`.

### Proposed fix

Add `_validate_stop_token_ids` to `SamplingParams` mirroring `_validate_logit_bias`, rejecting out-of-vocab ids with a 400 before the request reaches the engine. PR to follow.

When a structured-output request's drafts are lost that way, its `-1` placeholders survive into `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask`, which then writes `_full_mask` — **every token in the vocabulary allowed** — at rows that are real sampling positions. The worker verifies the genuine drafts from its own GPU-resident copy, so acceptance can walk straight into those rows and emit up to `num_speculative_tokens` tokens with no grammar constraint at all. The failure is silent by construction: the mask fails **open**. When the emitted tokens happen to be grammar-legal the request is quietly corrupted and keeps generating from a poisoned context; when they are not, the request dies with ``` ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py] Failed to advance FSM for request for tokens . ERROR [scheduler.py] Unexpected: grammar rejected tokens [30, 128825, ...] for request . Terminating request. ``` **This is latent on `main` today** — see "Reachability" below. It becomes live the moment a pipeline-parallel-capable drafter lands, which is why it seems worth fixing before that happens rather than after. All line numbers below are `main` @ `87b9b5b`. ### The chain **1. The scheduler installs `-1` placeholders for the next step's drafts.** `vllm/v1/core/sched/async_scheduler.py:42-44` ```python # Add placeholders for the new draft/spec tokens. # We will update the actual spec token ids in the worker process. request.spec_token_ids = self._spec_token_placeholders # [-1] * K ``` **2. They are back-filled from a single, unidentified slot.** The deferred-sampling branch (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py:678`, back-fill at `:736`) calls `take_draft_token_ids()`, which resolves to `DraftTokensHandler` (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/utils.py:11`): ```python def set_draft_tokens(self, input_batch, draft_tokens) -> None: self.req_ids = input_batch.req_ids # :25 — overwritten every step self.num_draft_tokens = draft_tokens.shape[1] if not input_batch.has_structured_output_reqs: self.draft_tokens_np = None # and cleared by plain batches return ``` No step id, no batch id, no history. The slot is correct only when the batch that last reached the worker covers the same requests as the step being sampled. That holds at `pipeline_parallel_size == 1`, where `max_concurrent_batches` is 2 (`vllm/config/vllm.py:563`): the deferred branch pops one entry and blocks on it, and the slot ends up holding exactly the predecessor's drafts. Under pipeline parallelism it does not hold. `max_concurrent_batches` becomes `pp_size + 1`, and `next_decode_eligible_step = current_step + pp_size` (`async_scheduler.py:48`) alternates requests across microbatches, so the batch that wrote the slot is a *different request set* than the one being sampled. There is also a second, more direct path (`utils.py:48-51`): ```python else: # This case only happens when async scheduling is disabled. draft_token_ids = [[-1] * self.num_draft_tokens for _ in self.req_ids] ``` That comment is not accurate: the branch is taken whenever the last batch to reach `set_draft_tokens` had no structured-output requests, which a plain-only microbatch does routinely. **3. A surviving `-1` makes the bitmask fail open.** `vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py:301-306` ```python for i, token in enumerate(req_tokens): self._fill_bitmasks(((grammar, cumulative_index, apply_bitmask),)) # row i filled FIRST advance_grammar = apply_bitmask if token == -1: # :304 apply_bitmask = False # rows i+1.. get _full_mask advance_grammar = False ``` `_full_mask` is `torch.tensor(-1, dtype=torch.int32)` — 32 bits set (`:59`, applied at `:213`) — and `apply_grammar_bitmask` only writes `-inf` where a bit is **0**. "The mask could not be built" therefore renders as "every token is allowed". Note that row 0 is filled *before* `req_tokens[0]` is inspected, so it is always correct. Only rows `1..K-1` go permissive. **4. Meanwhile the model verifies the real drafts, not the `-1`s.** The `-1` exists only in the scheduler's copy. The worker builds `input_ids` from its own GPU-resident `req_states.draft_tokens` via `combine_sampled_and_draft_tokens`, so the rejection sampler verifies genuine draft tokens against rows whose mask allows everything. We hit the symptom in production because our deployment carries a local relaxation for a side-model drafter (a DSpark head, which runs on the last stage rather than being partitioned across stages) plus the PP plumbing to broadcast draft tokens between stages. Any upstream change that makes a side-model drafter work under PP — which seems a natural thing to want — turns this from latent into live. ### Field evidence (from that deployment) 2 nodes x 2 GPUs, `pipeline_parallel_size=2`, `tensor_parallel_size=2`, DeepSeek-V4-Flash with `dspark` K=7, xgrammar backend. | probe | result | |---|---| | `tool_choice=required`, solo into an idle engine | passes 3/3 | | `tool_choice=required`, one other grammar request decoding | **fails 3/3** | | `json_schema` | **fails** | | `tool_choice=auto`, `json_object`, plain text | passes (permissive grammar hides it) | | `temperature=0` | passes (the resample kernel returns early on the masked argmax) | | speculative decoding disabled | passes | Permissive grammars pass because an unconstrained token is usually still legal, which is why this presents for a long time as "one agent out of six occasionally emits garbage" rather than as a hard error. Instrumenting `update_draft_token_ids_in_output` to classify each structured-output request in the deferred `SchedulerOutput` (6 concurrent `tool_choice=required` requests, 2400+ deferred steps): ``` MISSING (absent from draft_token_ids.req_ids) 100% ALL_MINUS1 (present, all drafts -1) 0% REAL ~0% ``` Retaining the last 4 snapshots and reporting at what depth the request's drafts would have been found: ``` MISSING@depth1 == MISSING 100% ``` The drafts are never actually unavailable — they are exactly one snapshot away, 100% of the time, which is the signature of a single slot under alternating PP microbatches. Solo, the back-fill succeeds ~85% of the time, which is why this only shows up under concurrency. Histogram of where the first `-1` lands in the K=7 window, same load: ``` first -1 at index -> {0: 2710, 1: 6, 2: 4, 3: 3, 4: 4, 5: 21, 6: 12, 7: 1309} ``` 66% of grammar rows had no usable draft at all, i.e. rows 1..7 permissive. ### Relationship to made the **bonus** row stay constrained after `-1` padding, and `tests/v1/spec_decode/test_mtp_structured_output.py:144` asserts exactly that: ```python assert not (bitmask[-1] == -1).all() ``` Rows `1..K-1` are deliberately left permissive, on the assumption that a `-1` means "this draft was rejected by `validate_tokens`, so the sampler will reject it too". That assumption is sound when the `-1` really is a rejection signal. It is violated here, where `-1` means "the drafts never reached the scheduler" — and no test covers those rows. `rejection_sampler_utils.py:767` already resamples a `-1` position straight from the target distribution and needs no change. ### Suggested fix Two independent pieces; the first is the correctness fix and stands alone. 1. **Fail closed.** When a structured-output request's scheduled spec tokens still contain `-1` at index `j`, mark drafts `j..K-1` invalid (`is_valid_draft = draft_sampled >= 0`) so the accepted length cannot run past the last row with a real mask. Rows `0..j` are correctly masked, so row `j` still supplies the step's token under the right constraint. Cost: that step gets no speculative speed-up. 2. **Give the hand-off an identity.** Snapshot `req_states.draft_tokens` where `prepare_inputs` feeds it into `input_ids` — at *consumption* time, not proposal time — tagged with the scheduler's step counter, and retain the last few. The scheduler then asks for the snapshot belonging to the step it is sampling, by equality, instead of taking whatever ran last. A miss falls back to (1), so the failure mode is the conservative one rather than a wrong mask. Both are implemented and running in our deployment. Measured effect of (2) on top of (1), 5 concurrent requests, aggregate decode throughput: | grammar + plain | (1) only | (1)+(2) | |---|---|---| | 1 + 4 | 235.6 | 256.0 | | 3 + 2 | 170.7 | 260.2 | | 5 + 0 | 111.9 | **276.8** | With (2), grammar requests decode at 52–58 tok/s against a 52.5 tok/s plain-text baseline — the speculative speed-up is fully recovered. Back-fill hit rate goes to 100%, and bitmask rows carrying a real mask from 32% to 96.5%. Happy to open PRs for both if this looks like the right direction. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Searched existing issues and asked the documentation chatbot.

[Bug][DCP] GLM-5.3 dense prefill consumes uninitialized K rows on non-owner ranks

### Problem

Following the GLM-5.3 report in , TP4/DCP4 generation with Inferact/GLM-5.3-NVFP4 is deterministically incoherent while matched TP4/DCP1 is coherent. This remains after applying the earlier correctness fix and after disabling the direct DCP communication paths, so it is a separate bug.
The GLM-5.3 problem is originally reported by @ehfd 

### Root cause

NVIDIA DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5.3 dense prefill requests normalized/rotated K materialization from fused_norm_rope on every DCP rank. The fused kernel currently returns when slot_mapping is negative. Under DCP, a negative local slot can mean that another rank owns the cache row; it does not mean that the dense-prefill K row is unused. As a result, non-owner ranks leave kv_c_out and k_pe_out uninitialized, and dense prefill consumes those buffers.

Cache ownership and K materialization need separate guards: materialize the requested K outputs on every rank, but retain the negative-slot guard before owner-local cache writes.

### Validation

On 4x GB200 with greedy decoding, chunked prefill, prefix caching, FP8 KV cache, and CUDA graphs enabled, the narrow fix makes DCP4 token output exactly match DCP1 for:

- 512 uncached prompt tokens: SHA256 222258a1...
- 1536 uncached prompt tokens: SHA256 76643708...
- 1024 cached plus 1536 uncached prompt tokens: SHA256 4a150ea6...

The model run used the matching cu130 binary/source pair at 570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e with and the narrow fix overlaid. The same failing guard is unchanged on current main ee3c00bbf47e0ef7e975705cc980b06ee5576bb0; a current-main native build is still in progress and will be added to the PR validation.

A focused current-main regression test also passes and verifies that K outputs are materialized while MLA/indexer caches remain untouched on a non-owner rank.

No open PR was found for 50095 or for this GLM-5.3 DCP materialization bug before filing. AI assistance was used for diagnosis, implementation, and validation; the human submitter will review the patch before marking the PR ready.

[Bug] Qwen4Exp QSA indexer: per-chunk logits buffer grows with max_seq_len, caching allocator keeps every size, device OOM/hang on unified-memory GB10 (SM121) during long prefill

## Your current environment

- vLLM `0.28.1rc1.dev628+g2a02f6efe` (nightly image `vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:96b234afa2867031ad0a226b149a06483861e613e3a3083da53398d347b5ffbd`, arm64), CUDA 13, V2 model runner.
- 2× NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, SM121, **unified memory**, 119 GB each), TP=2 across the two nodes (Ray-less multi-node, `--nnodes 2`).
- Model: `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (Qwen4Exp architecture: 12 QSA sparse-attention layers with indexer, 36 GDN layers, PLE), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--max-model-len 262144`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096`, chunked prefill, prefix caching, MTP k=3, `cudagraph_mode FULL_DECODE_ONLY`, `gpu_memory_utilization 0.8`.
- `indexer_compress_ratio=4`, `indexer_budget=2048` (model config). KV block size on this hybrid: 3200 tokens.
- Note: we run a few local overlays on top of this nightly (fp8 KV for QSA from , a refusal-direction hook), but `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ops/qsa_indexer.py` (the code path below) is unmodified upstream. The previous nightly we ran (`8a728663`, `0.28.1rc1.dev388`) does not show the problem with the same model, hardware and flags.

## 🐛 Describe the bug

A single 254K-token cold prefill kills the engine on GB10: the step hangs at exactly **166,400 computed tokens**, the driver logs `NVRM: nvCheckOkFailedNoLog: Check failed: Out of memory [NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY] ... _memdescAllocInternal(pMemDesc) @ mem_desc.c:1359` on both nodes, and after 300 s the EngineCore dies with `TimeoutError: RPC call to sample_tokens timed out.` (dumped `SchedulerOutput`: `num_computed_tokens=[..., 166400]`, `num_scheduled_tokens={...: 3200}`).

Node-exporter shows each rank consuming ~9–14 GB **outside the KV pool** during the last ~60 s of the prefill (worker 13 → 4 GB available, head 9 → 0 GB), whereas on `8a728663` the same prefill leaves memory flat.

### Root cause

`qsa_select_paged_prefill` in `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ops/qsa_indexer.py` now sizes the indexer logits buffer by the batch's `max_seq_len`:

```python
logits_width = triton.cdiv(triton.cdiv(max_seq_len, compress_ratio), 64) * 64
logits_width = min(max(64, logits_width), page_table.shape[1] * k_cache.shape[1])
max_logits_bytes = envs.VLLM_SPARSE_INDEXER_MAX_LOGITS_MB * 1024 * 1024 # 512 MB default
rows_per_chunk = max(1, max_logits_bytes // (logits_width * 4))
...
logits = torch.empty((num_queries, logits_width), dtype=torch.float32, ...)
```

Previously (`8a728663`) the width was the fixed page-table width (`columns = page_table.shape[1] * k_cache.shape[1]`), so every chunk allocated the same 512 MB buffer and the caching allocator reused it.

With chunked prefill (3200-token chunks here) and `compress_ratio=4`, chunk *i* of a long prompt now allocates `3200 × (800·i) × 4 B = 10.24 MB × i`, a **strictly increasing** size per chunk, until 3200 rows no longer fit under the 512 MB cap: `i = 52` → `52 × 3200 = 166,400 tokens`, exactly where the engine died. The PyTorch caching allocator never finds a cached block large enough for the next request, so it `cudaMalloc`s a new one each chunk and keeps the previous ones: `Σ 10.24 MB × i (i ≤ 52) ≈ 14 GB per rank`. On a discrete GPU `cudaMalloc` would eventually fail and the allocator would flush its cache and retry; on unified-memory GB10 `cudaMalloc` keeps succeeding until the driver has nothing left, and the failure surfaces as a GPU hang (`NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY` in dmesg) instead of a Python OOM.

### Evidence

- Attempt 1 (defaults): hang at 166,400 tokens, `NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY` ×7 on the worker node at the hang time, EngineCore dead 300 s later.
- Attempt 2 (`gdn_prefill_backend=triton`, to rule out the new FlashInfer GDN prefill path on SM12x): node memory still dropping during the prefill (head 9 → 6 GB in 49 s), probe aborted by a watchdog. GDN kernel is not the cause.
- Attempt 3 (`VLLM_SPARSE_INDEXER_MAX_LOGITS_MB=64`): the per-chunk request saturates at ~21K tokens (chunk 7) and is reused from there. Memory flat for the whole 254K prefill and for 8 concurrent 254K prompts; no errors. The cold prefill is even ~10% faster than on `8a728663` (92 s vs ~102 s single 254K prompt).

### Workaround

`VLLM_SPARSE_INDEXER_MAX_LOGITS_MB=64` (cost: up to 8 kernel launches per chunk and layer at 166K context instead of 1).

### Suggested fix

Round `logits_width` up to coarse buckets (e.g. multiples of 16K compressed columns), or allocate the buffer once at the page-table width as before, or take it from the workspace manager, so the caching allocator can reuse one block across chunks. Any allocation whose size grows monotonically per chunk will reproduce this on unified-memory devices.
